summary: The article compares Literary and Media Production workshops run in global education systems since September 2023, showing how storytelling in student projects differs by continent. North America stresses personal narratives, Europe history and myth, Africa communal oral traditions, Asia ancient philosophy with contemporary issues, and Australia technology like VR and AR. It concludes that despite differing methods, all aim to tell a story that matters.
one_line: Workshops launched since September 2023 reveal how storytelling in student media projects varies across North America, Europe, Africa, Asia and Australia.
key_facts: Literary and Media Production workshops have been held in educational institutions worldwide since September 2023.
Elizabeth Monroe, a celebrated author and educator from Harvard, began US workshops on October 5, 2023, focusing on developing individual voices through personal experience.
Students in Monroe's workshops created documentaries, short films, and podcasts reflecting their own lives.
Henrik Vogler, a Swedish film director, has guided young creatives in Stockholm since September 16, 2023, in weaving ancestral legends with modern dilemmas.
European student work includes animated shorts, theatrical performances, and virtual reality experiences adapting classic folklore; Vogler says "In Europe, our past informs our future."
Amina Okoye, an educator and storyteller, launched workshops in Nairobi on November 3, 2023, embodying Ubuntu – "I am because we are."
Students in Okoye's Nairobi workshops collaboratively developed scripts for radio plays and web series.
Kenji Tanaka, a manga artist and philosopher, has led workshops in Japan since September 23, 2023, using manga to discuss environmentalism and social structure.
Connor Macleod, a digital media expert, started courses in Melbourne on September 30, 2023, emphasizing virtual reality, augmented reality, and interactive storytelling.
Australian projects include VR experiences that transport users into narratives and AR apps that bring stories into users' environments.

The article summarizes the regional emphases as North American individual agency, European historical allegories, African communal oral traditions, Asian philosophic art, and Australian technology-infused tales.
The article concludes that the shared goal across regions is "to tell a story that matters," with multimedia platforms serving as vessels for stories.
